clue.text: Hope for a high church position

blocks.note: taken as written
the tall pointed top of a church tower sits high above it

explanation.surface: An ambitious cleric dreams of promotion to a lofty post in the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High church position' looks like a bishopric or similar office; read literally it is the topmost part of a church building.
explanation.definitionFit: To aspire is to set one's heart on achieving something, an ambition or longing for success.

clue.text: There's nothing dull in a swell perfume

indicators.note: the nothing and dull pieces go inside the swell

blocks.note: taken as written
a rise is a swelling, as of the sea or ground
zero, the letter O
a matt finish is dull, not glossy, also spelt mat

explanation.surface: A dandy's scent is anything but dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swell' looks like a fashionable gentleman; it is a rise. 'Perfume' looks like a noun but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To aromatise is to give something a pleasant fragrance, just as to perfume it is to scent it.

clue.text: A minor deity longing for real style

blocks.note: Pan is the Greek god of shepherds and the wild, a minor god
to ache for something is to long for it

explanation.surface: A lesser god yearns to have genuine flair.
explanation.definitionFit: Panache is dash and flamboyant confidence, the quality of having genuine flair in how one acts.

clue.text: Difficulty with raciest characters makes the reader see red

indicators.note: the word is treated as mere characters, letters free to be set out in a new order

blocks.note: as in 'there's the rub', a snag
taken as written

explanation.surface: Racy characters in a book shock a prim reader into fury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See red' sounds like anger; literally it is red ink, as in the red headings of old manuscripts.
explanation.definitionFit: To rubricate is to mark or print text in red, the colour of medieval headings, so a reader literally sees red.

clue.text: Repeatedly. Charlie batting sees bumper off

indicators.note: says the next word's letters are to be used twice in a row

blocks.note: a charlie is British slang for a fool
the same fool a second time
a cricket side batting is said to be in

explanation.surface: A batsman called Charlie keeps being hit by a short-pitched bouncer from a fast bowler.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a bumper is a fast ball that rears up at the batsman; here 'bumper off' is one who bumps people off, i.e. kills them.
explanation.definitionFit: To bump someone off is slang for murdering them, so a bumper off is a hired killer.

clue.text: Restricted in way one course can lead to another

definitions.text: Restricted in way one course can lead to another

blocks.clueFragment: Restricted in way one course can lead to another
blocks.note: surface reading: a narrow road where one racecourse or watercourse runs on into a second

blocks.clueFragment: one course can lead to another
blocks.note: setter's reading: the dessert course written first and followed by the main course, making a word for a small confection

explanation.surface: A narrow lane joins one golf or racecourse to the next.
explanation.walkthrough: The courses are a meal's: the pudding placed ahead of the main dish. How 'Restricted in way' fits is unclear; perhaps that the word only works in this restricted order.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweetmeat is an item of confectionery, a candied delicacy, and literally the sweet course leading the meat course.

clue.text: Taking a chance, offer support

blocks.note: taken as written
a bet is a chance taken on an outcome

explanation.surface: A gambler backs a horse, risking money on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking a chance' reads as one phrase for gambling; split, it is a plus a word for a wager.
explanation.definitionFit: To abet is to help or encourage someone, usually in wrongdoing, as in aiding and abetting.

clue.text: Clothing that fits one to a T

blocks.note: single means one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A garment that suits its wearer perfectly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To a T' is an idiom for exactly; here T is just the letter added after the piece for one.
explanation.definitionFit: A singlet is a sleeveless vest worn as underwear or by athletes, an item of clothing.

clue.text: Direction given by the prime minister at one time

definitions.text: the prime minister at one time

blocks.note: first meaning: a compass point, opposite south

blocks.clueFragment: the prime minister at one time
blocks.note: second meaning: Lord ___, Britain's prime minister when the American colonies were lost

explanation.surface: An instruction issued by a former head of government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Direction' reads as an order from the PM; it is a compass bearing.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a cardinal compass point and the title of Frederick Lord North, British premier from 1770 to 1782.

clue.text: The Spanish and Italian agreement upset 15, say

indicators.note: in a down entry, upset means turned upside down, so the letters read from the bottom

blocks.note: el is Spanish for the
si is Italian for yes

explanation.surface: A treaty between Spain and Italy angers a third nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 15 across is IRELAND, an example of the answer, hence 'say'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ireland is an island, and isle is a poetic word for an island.

clue.text: Volume of city traffic

blocks.note: first meaning: a book collecting several works in one binding
second meaning: the old full name of the bus, a large vehicle on urban streets

explanation.surface: A complaint about how loud or heavy the traffic in town is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Volume of' reads as an amount of traffic; volume is really a book.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a collected edition of a writer's works and the public road vehicle later shortened to bus.

clue.text: Regal lady who got cross at every halt, being late

definitions.text: Regal lady who got cross at every halt, being late

blocks.clueFragment: Regal lady who got cross at every halt, being late
blocks.note: surface reading: an impatient royal grew angry at each stop because she was running behind time

blocks.clueFragment: got cross at every halt, being late
blocks.note: setter's reading: after this queen died, her grieving husband put up a stone monument at each place her funeral procession rested overnight

explanation.surface: A queen loses her temper whenever her journey stops, because she is behind schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward I raised a series of stone crosses, such as Charing Cross in London, at the resting places of his dead wife's cortege; 'late' means dead, not tardy.
explanation.definitionFit: She was Edward I's queen, a royal consort, so a regal lady, commemorated by the famous crosses named after her.

clue.text: Those who plan the Arctic's development

indicators.note: a development of something is a reworked form of it, so the letters before it are rebuilt

blocks.note: the words taken letter for letter, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Planners mapping out how the polar north will be built up and exploited.
explanation.definitionFit: Architects draw up the designs for buildings, and figuratively anyone who devises a scheme is its architect.

clue.text: Black Prince retreating? Non-sense!

indicators.note: something retreating goes back the way it came, so the prince is read from the end

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
Prince Hal is Shakespeare's name for the young Henry V

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at the claim that the Black Prince ever ran from battle.
explanation.walkthrough: The Black Prince was Edward III's warrior son; the phrase must be split, black and prince giving separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Blah is empty, meaningless talk, the sort of drivel that makes no sense at all.

clue.text: Timekeeper given very little help

blocks.note: minute (pronounced my-newt) means tiny
to give someone a hand is to help them

explanation.surface: A referee or official timekeeper gets almost no assistance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Timekeeper' suggests a person at a sports event; it is part of a clock.
explanation.definitionFit: The long pointer on a clock face marks the minutes, so it is a part that keeps time.

clue.text: Anger sovereign and country

blocks.note: ire is a literary word for anger
a sovereign is a gold pound coin, and L stands for pound
taken as written

explanation.surface: Fury at both the monarch and the nation, as if from a rebel.
explanation.walkthrough: A sovereign was a British gold coin worth one pound, and L (from Latin libra) is the pound sign's letter.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an island nation west of Great Britain, so a country by any measure.

clue.text: Dunderhead is proceeding to make speech

blocks.note: read as dunder-head, the head or first letter of dunder
taken as written
a course is a way of proceeding, as in 'in the course of'

explanation.surface: An idiot heads to the podium to give an address.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dunderhead' looks like an insult; split, it gives the first letter of dunder.
explanation.definitionFit: A discourse is a formal spoken or written treatment of a subject, such as a lecture or sermon.

clue.text: Met with diet problem, so put out

indicators.note: a problem leaves things in a mess, so the letters before it come out jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone ran into trouble with their eating plan and was left upset about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' looks like annoyed, matching the diet trouble; it is used in the sense of sent forth.
explanation.definitionFit: Emitted means gave off or released, as light, sound or gas is put out by a source.

clue.text: Cleaning put off bloke

blocks.note: to deter is to discourage
short for gentleman; bloke is British slang for a man

explanation.surface: A man is discouraged from doing the housework.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective, detergent describes something that cleanses, as a soap or washing agent does.

clue.text: Title for a newspaper, say

blocks.note: first meaning: the name of a British national daily, the Daily ___
second meaning: to put into words, to state

explanation.surface: Someone suggests a possible masthead name for a new paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like 'for example'; it is a verb meaning to voice. The Daily Express is a long-running British tabloid.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a well-known British paper's name and a verb meaning to convey a thought in words.

clue.text: Coppers like a period for recreation

blocks.note: copper coins are pence, abbreviated p
as means like, in the manner of
a time is a period

explanation.surface: Policemen enjoy a spell of leisure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coppers' suggests police; it means copper coins, British pennies, written p.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastime is a hobby or activity done for enjoyment in one's leisure hours.

clue.text: Bellow, or maybe mutter, about parking

indicators.note: says the word that follows is just one possible form, so its letters may be arranged otherwise
the shuffled word goes round, about, the next piece

blocks.note: taken as written
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: An angry driver either shouts or grumbles about finding a parking space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bellow' and 'mutter' look like two ways of complaining; only the first is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To trumpet is to roar loudly like an elephant, so it can stand for bellow as a verb.

clue.text: Quiet and exceptionally petite dispenser

indicators.note: something done exceptionally departs from the normal, so the letters leave their usual order

blocks.note: p is the musical marking piano, quietly
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shy, very small woman hands things out.
explanation.definitionFit: A pipette is a slender laboratory tube that measures out and releases small quantities of liquid.

clue.text: Firm call to stop talking in the club

blocks.note: Co. is the abbreviation for company
the sound made to hush someone

explanation.surface: A stern request for silence in a gentlemen's club reading room.
explanation.walkthrough: A cosh is a British word for a short heavy truncheon; 'Firm' looks like an adjective for the call but is a business.
explanation.definitionFit: A cosh is a short weighted bludgeon, a weapon of exactly the kind called a club.

clue.text: Class a godly person held in church

indicators.note: says the godly person sits inside the church

blocks.note: CE is the Church of England
taken as written
a saint, abbreviated St

explanation.surface: A devout parishioner sits in a pew among the congregation of a particular rank.
explanation.definitionFit: A caste is a hereditary social rank, as in the traditional Hindu system of social groups.

clue.text: Librarian who ensures all returns are duly dealt with?

definitions.text: Librarian who ensures all returns are duly dealt with?

blocks.clueFragment: Librarian who ensures all returns are duly dealt with
blocks.note: surface reading: a library assistant who checks in every borrowed volume brought back
setter's reading: tax returns and financial accounts, kept in order by someone who maintains a firm's ledgers

explanation.surface: A conscientious library worker processes every returned book promptly.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the librarian is a joke: the answer read in two halves sounds like someone who keeps books.
explanation.definitionFit: This clerk records a business's transactions in its account books, and literally a person who holds on to books.

clue.text: Show affection for “X"

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb, to touch with the lips fondly
second meaning: the cross written at the end of a letter as a token of love

explanation.walkthrough: X written at the end of a card or letter stands for this, so the letter itself is a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both the act of touching lips in love and the name of the X mark signed under a note.

clue.text: One provides small but useful holding, in perpetuity

definitions.text: One provides small but useful holding

indicators.note: says the letters are held within the next word

blocks.note: the four letters from the middle of the word

explanation.surface: A modest but handy property owned for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holding' sounds like a landholding or investment; the definition means a small case holding things.
explanation.definitionFit: An etui is a small ornamental case for carrying needles, scissors or toiletries, a compact container.

clue.text: Quicker to see point in a riddle

indicators.note: says the point goes inside the riddle

blocks.note: a riddle is a coarse sieve, something that sifts
a compass point, west

explanation.surface: A sharp mind gets the joke of a puzzle faster than others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riddle' looks like a puzzle; it is the gardener's sieve for soil or gravel.
explanation.definitionFit: Swifter is the comparative of swift, meaning faster or more rapid.

clue.text: Arrange about a place in America

indicators.note: the first word wraps round, about, the single letter after it

blocks.note: to settle a matter is to arrange it
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone organising the details of a location somewhere in the USA.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the largest city in Washington State in the Pacific Northwest of the United States.

clue.text: They're on their own before the children appear

blocks.note: ere is a poetic word for before
mites are small children

explanation.surface: A couple enjoys some time alone before the kids turn up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appear' just places the children after the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Eremites are hermits, religious recluses who live in solitude away from society.

clue.text: Some hundreds in a hole before Christmas

definitions.note: a phrase standing for the noun, the period before Christmas

indicators.note: says the hundreds are placed inside the hole

blocks.note: taken as written
a vent is an opening that lets air or smoke out
D is the Roman numeral for five hundred, several hundreds

explanation.surface: Plenty of people end up in financial trouble in the run-up to Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some hundreds in a hole' sounds like debt; D, the Roman 500, is literally some hundreds.
explanation.definitionFit: Advent is the season of the church year covering the four weeks leading up to the Nativity feast.
